title: Find the Point: Central Ideas and Details
description: Use Find the Point to distinguish a whole-text central idea from a requested detail, preserve qualifications, and match a supported paraphrase.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first choice and what made it seem plausible. You can continue without submitting an answer.

  1. The museum’s labels continue to identify when its vessels were made and which potters produced them.
  2. Trial pieces and firing notes document temperature adjustments that one potter made while developing a polished jar.
  3. The gallery compares similar-looking bowls to show that different makers can arrive at related forms through different experiments.
  4. The gallery presents finished vessels alongside evidence of their making, directing attention to how potters developed their results.

shared_prompt.title: A redesigned pottery gallery
shared_prompt.html: A museum once grouped ceramic vessels by date and region. In its redesigned gallery, a polished jar stands next to three misshapen trial versions, while firing notes document how the potter changed temperature between attempts. Labels still identify each finished piece’s date and maker, but they also connect its surface to choices recorded in the notes. Elsewhere, two similar-looking bowls appear beside records showing that their makers reached those forms through different experiments. The museum has kept its permanent collection while giving visitors more material to examine beside each finished object.

content.html:
A true detail can still be too small

The museum choices each describe something in the passage. The challenge is choosing the answer that covers what those details build together.

We’ll practise Find the Point: let the question decide the size of your answer. Start with a shorter passage about a garden.

What would you tell a friend?

Read the garden passage. Say its whole point in one sentence. Would mentioning only the seedlings tell your friend what changed about the garden’s value?

content.hint: Keep the original purpose and the new value together.
content.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The garden teaches children to grow vegetables for the local food pantry.
The garden now provides social connections as well as food.
The garden has replaced vegetable growing with meetings for exchanging recipes.
The garden’s larger harvests have attracted more residents to visit.
content.solution: Identify the original role: supplying food. Identify the added role: bringing neighbors together. Combine them: the garden now serves both food and social purposes. That is choice B.
content.explanation: The point is the garden’s expanded value. Seedlings are one detail; the text never says that food production stopped or increased.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: A neighborhood garden was originally planted to supply vegetables to a food pantry. Its harvests remain modest, but residents now gather there to exchange recipes and teach children to grow seedlings. The garden has become as valuable as a meeting place as it is as a source of food.

content.html:
Topic, point, and detail

The topic is the subject: a garden. The central idea is what the passage says about it: its value has expanded. A detail, such as exchanging recipes, helps support that idea.

content.hint: Look for a statement of what happened, not a label for what is discussed.
content.prompt: An essay explains that a theater’s low-cost afternoon performances attracted people who had never attended before. Which option is a central idea rather than a topic label?
choices: The afternoon performance schedule at a neighborhood theater
The low prices for the theater’s afternoon performances
The theater’s new audience members at afternoon performances
Lower prices brought the theater new audiences
content.solution: The last option says what the text communicates about the theater. The others only name subjects or details.
content.explanation: The last option says what the text communicates about the theater. The others only name subjects or details.

content.html:
Find the Point

  1. Check whether the question asks for the whole message or a specific detail.
  2. Read for the important ideas.
  3. Say the answer in your own words.
  4. Match its meaning and limits to a choice.

Connect the important ideas

The archive has fragile maps; scanning makes them easier to access; repairs continue. Together, those ideas suggest this target: scanning expands access while physical repair continues. A fact about the number of maps is too small for the main idea.

content.hint: Match both access and continuing repair; avoid adding a reason for the repair order.
content.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Scanning expands access while map repairs continue.
Archivists prioritized popular maps because they were most damaged.
Scanning has removed the need for the archive’s physical repairs.
The archive’s most important task is repairing damaged map edges.
content.solution: Size the question as whole-text. Combine scanning with the final sentence: digital access now works even when maps remain fragile, and repairs continue. Only A keeps both parts.
content.explanation: The first choice preserves the change and its limit. The last choice gives background; the middle choices add an unsupported cause or overstate the effect.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: The town archive holds hundreds of maps, many with damaged edges. Archivists first repaired the maps that visitors requested most often, leaving rarer maps in storage. A new scanning program now allows visitors to examine the fragile maps digitally without handling the originals. Repairs continue, but access no longer depends on a map being sturdy enough to unfold.

content.html:
Now zoom in

A detail question asks for one fact or relationship. Locate the requested evidence and read around it. Your answer can paraphrase that evidence; it does not need to summarize the whole passage.

content.hint: Locate the sentence that names the repair priority.
content.prompt: According to the text, which maps did the archivists repair first?
choices: Those that visitors asked to see most frequently
Those whose edges had the most severe damage
Those that were too large to scan digitally
Those that had remained in storage the longest
content.solution: The question asks about repair order, not scanning. The second sentence says visitors’ most-requested maps were repaired first. Match that frequency relationship to A.
content.explanation: “Requested most often” means asked to see most frequently. Severity, size, and time in storage are not the stated selection rule.

content.html:
Keep the limits

“More first-time visitors in this trial” does not mean “more visitors everywhere.” Keep limits about the group, time, and result when you shorten a passage. A choice needs support for its full claim.

content.hint: Keep the measured group, the comparison, and the trial’s time limit.
content.prompt: Which statement is supported by the text?
choices: Evening workshops brought more first-time visitors to the other branches too.
Evening workshops drew a larger total audience than morning workshops.
The trial’s evening workshops drew more first-time visitors.
Morning workshop attendance declined as the trial continued.
content.solution: Keep who was counted: first-time visitors. Keep where and when: one library’s six-week trial. Keep the direction: evening exceeds morning. C preserves all three.
content.explanation: The text compares first-time visitors during one trial. It does not compare every visitor, establish a weekly trend, or cover other libraries.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: During a six-week trial, a library’s evening workshops attracted more first-time visitors than its morning workshops. Attendance at both types of workshop varied from week to week.

content.html:
A contrast can carry the point

Words such as but and although connect an earlier idea with a change or limit. Include both sides when the passage’s main point depends on that relationship.

content.hint: Preserve the change in how critics assessed the same feature.
content.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea?
choices: Reviewers disagreed about which character should narrate the novel.
Later readers valued a feature earlier reviewers criticized.
Later critics considered the events less convincing than early reviewers did.
The author made the novel clearer by removing several narrators.
content.solution: Early view: multiple narrators are confusing. Later view: those shifts reveal different interpretations. Combine the two evaluations into B.
content.explanation: The narrators remain the same; the evaluation changes. The other choices invent a revision or misstate what the critics discuss.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: Although early reviewers called the novel’s many narrators confusing, later critics argued that the shifts in viewpoint reveal how differently the characters interpret the same event.

content.html:
For a scene, follow the reaction

A story may show an attitude through small actions. Ask what the character notices, does, or changes. Use those details to form your target without inventing a backstory.

content.hint: Compare her original intention with what she actually does.
content.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Mara is frustrated that repairing her old radio has taken so much time.
Mara discovers that her new speaker cannot receive her favorite station.
Mara decides that older technology produces clearer sound than newer technology.
Mara feels drawn to a familiar object despite having planned to replace it.
content.solution: Find the initial intention: discard the radio. Track the action: she sits and waits for a familiar tune. D captures that attachment without inventing a technical judgment.
content.explanation: Her plan to discard the radio gives way to listening. The new speaker is unopened, so no comparison of performance has occurred.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: Mara had meant to discard the old radio. Yet when its dial lit up, she settled beside it, listening through the hiss until the familiar evening tune began. The unopened box for her new speaker remained on the table.

content.html:
Match relationships, not repeated words

Check who does what and how the parts relate. A choice can use the passage’s nouns while changing the meaning. The right choice keeps the relationship even when its wording changes.

content.hint: Check the source of the words and the difference between near and distant viewing.
content.prompt: Which choice best describes the artist’s approach, as presented in the text?
choices: The artist lets residents choose colors for murals about neighborhood history.
The artist rewrites existing mural scenes as accounts of residents’ lives.
The artist combines residents’ words with images read differently at different distances.
The artist records residents’ conversations to demonstrate agreement about neighborhood art.
content.solution: Locate the action: collecting phrases and painting them. Locate the effect: color bands from far away, readable remarks nearby. C preserves both.
content.explanation: The words come from residents, and the viewing distance changes what viewers perceive. The text does not say residents choose colors or agree.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: An artist collects short phrases from neighborhood conversations and paints them into large murals. From a distance, the phrases blend into broad bands of color. Up close, viewers can read individual remarks about work, school, and family. The artist uses this shift in scale to connect a neighborhood’s collective appearance with the lives of its residents.

blocks.html:
Return to the museum

Try the opening passage again. Form an answer target that fits the question before comparing the choices.

content.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The museum’s labels continue to identify when its vessels were made and which potters produced them.
Trial pieces and firing notes document temperature adjustments that one potter made while developing a polished jar.
The gallery compares similar-looking bowls to show that different makers can arrive at related forms through different experiments.
The gallery presents finished vessels alongside evidence of their making, directing attention to how potters developed their results.
content.hint: Check the size of the task. What connects the jar, the notes, and the two bowls, rather than describing only one display?
content.solution:
The question asks for the whole text’s main idea, not a requested detail.
The displays pair finished vessels with evidence of the decisions and experiments behind them.
Use that connection as your target, then check which choice covers both examples and the gallery’s overall change.
Choose D.
A: This accurately describes the labels but leaves out the gallery’s new emphasis.
B: This is a supported example from one display, rather than the whole passage’s point.
C: This accurately describes the second display, but it does not cover the rest of the redesign.
content.explanation: That’s the whole point. The matching answer connects the displays; the other choices are accurate but narrower details.

content.prompt: You remember a striking detail, but the question asks for the main idea. What does Find the Point tell you to do?
choices: Discard the detail and assume the final sentence must contain the complete answer.
Choose the detail if its wording appears unchanged in one of the answer choices.
Combine the important ideas, predict the overall message, and test each choice against that scope.
Choose the broadest claim about the topic even if it extends beyond the passage.
content.explanation: Set the answer’s size from the question. A main idea is broad enough for the message and narrow enough for the evidence.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: According to the text, how did Elena handle conflicting memories?
choices: She kept both accounts and marked the identification unresolved.
She chose the account of the person who donated the photograph.
She accepted the earliest interview as the most reliable source.
She removed the disputed photographs from the neighborhood project.
content.explanation: Keeping both accounts and marking uncertainty matches A. The text specifies no rule for choosing one account or removing an image.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: For a neighborhood history project, Elena first cataloged photographs donated by residents. She then interviewed the donors to identify the streets and people in images with missing labels. When memories conflicted, she kept both accounts in the catalog and marked the identification as uncertain.

content.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The photographs show that species has little influence on street-tree growth.
Context about surroundings has improved the inventory’s planning value.
Volunteers have replaced the original tree measurements with building photographs.
Planners now rely on annual photographs instead of recording species and size.
content.explanation: The passage centers on enriching an existing record. A dismisses species without support, C falsely replaces the measurements, and D invents an annual requirement.

shared_prompt.title: Passage to use
shared_prompt.html: For years, a city’s tree inventory listed the species and location of each street tree but recorded little about its surroundings. A volunteer team recently added photographs showing pavement, nearby buildings, and the amount of open soil at each site. The photographs do not replace the original measurements. Instead, they supply context that helps planners interpret why trees of the same species may fare differently on neighboring streets. The revised inventory thus preserves a useful record while making it more informative for future planting decisions.

content.html:
Find the Point

Let the question set the size of your answer.
